Witness of the Spirit
WIT-nuhs of the SPIR-it
n. phrase
From Greek symmartyreō, to bear witness together with; the phrase rendering Paul's "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God" (Rom 8:16).

📖 Biblical Definition

The Witness of the Spirit is the gracious work of the Holy Ghost whereby He confirms to the believer's own consciousness that he is indeed a child of God, and so undergirds the assurance of salvation. The foundation text is Romans 8:16: "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God." The verb is symmartyreō, to witness together with: the Spirit does not testify in a vacuum, nor merely to us, but bears witness with our spirit, joining His testimony to the renewed conscience of the believer. Two witnesses thus concur—the Spirit and the saint's own spirit—and in the mouth of two witnesses the matter is established. This witness operates chiefly by enabling the believer to cry, "Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6), shedding abroad the love of God in the heart and giving a filial confidence toward God. It is crucial to mark what this witness is not. It is no fresh revelation, no audible voice, no new word added to Scripture telling the man his name is written in the book of life. This dictionary is cessationist: the Spirit gives no new inspired words. Rather, the Spirit's witness works through and by the word already given, applying its promises and its marks of grace to the heart, illuminating the evidences of regeneration that the word itself describes—love of the brethren, hatred of sin, delight in God's law, the keeping of His commandments—so that the believer, examining himself by Scripture and feeling the Spirit's seal upon the verdict, is assured. Assurance therefore rests on a threefold cord: the promises of the word, the fruits of grace in the life, and the witness of the Spirit confirming both. This dictionary confesses that the Spirit's witness is a real, sweet, and solid ground of assurance—not a mystical bypass of the word, but the Spirit's own amen, set upon His own written promises, in the heart of His own child.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WITNESS as testimony, attestation of a fact, and one who gives evidence. The Witness of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost's confirming testimony, joined to the believer's renewed spirit, that he is a child of God (Rom 8:16).

expand to see more

WITNESS, n. — Testimony; attestation of a fact or event. Also, one who knows or sees any thing; one personally present; one who gives testimony or evidence.

In the spiritual sense, the Witness of the Spirit is the Holy Ghost bearing witness together with the believer's spirit that he is a child of God.

"The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God" (Rom 8:16).

It requires that the saint ground assurance on the Spirit's confirming testimony joined to the word and the fruits of grace; it forbids resting on a fresh revelation or inward voice.

It is no new word added to Scripture, but the Spirit's amen set upon His own written promises in the heart of His child.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 8:16 — "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God."

Romans 8:15 — "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father."

Galatians 4:6 — "And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father."

1 John 4:13 — "Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he hath given us of his Spirit."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Witness of the Spirit is corrupted when it is treated as a fresh private revelation or an inward voice giving new information, rather than the Spirit's confirming testimony exercised through the closed and sufficient word.

expand to see more

The most common abuse turns the witness of the Spirit into a species of private revelation—an impression, an inward voice, a sudden conviction that descends upon the mind announcing "you are saved," received with the same authority as Scripture and beyond all examination. On this view assurance floats free of the word and of the fruits of grace, resting wholly on the strength of a feeling, so that a man may presume upon a comfortable impression while his life gives no evidence of regeneration. But Scripture knows no such bare witness. The Spirit bears witness with our spirit (Rom 8:16), joining His testimony to the renewed conscience as it judges the life by the marks of grace the word lays down; and John gives the test plainly: "hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments" (1 John 2:3). A witness that cannot bear the trial of the word and the life is no witness of the Holy Ghost.

Because this dictionary is cessationist, it denies that the Spirit's witness is any new inspired communication. The canon is closed; the Spirit speaks no fresh words. His witness is the application of the word already given—sealing the promises, illuminating the evidences, shedding abroad the love of God in the heart so that the believer cries Abba, Father with filial confidence. The recovery of the doctrine is to set the witness of the Spirit upon its proper foundation: the threefold cord of the promises of Scripture, the fruits of grace tried by self-examination, and the Spirit's confirming seal. So grounded, assurance is no presumption and no mysticism, but the solid joy of a child of God who has the Spirit's own amen upon the verdict of the word.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on Paul's to pneuma symmartyrei tōi pneumati hēmōn (Rom 8:16), the Spirit witnessing together with the believer's spirit, and the filial cry "Abba, Father."

expand to see more

Greek symmartyreō (G4828) — to bear witness together with; the verb of Rom 8:16, the Spirit testifying with our spirit.

Greek martyria (G3141) — witness, testimony; the legal-forensic background of two concurring witnesses establishing a matter.

Aramaic abba (G5) — father; the intimate filial address the Spirit of adoption enables (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6).

Greek plerophoria (G4136) — full assurance; the settled confidence the Spirit's witness produces in the heart.

The witness is no new revelation but the Spirit's confirming seal applied through the already-given and sufficient word.

Usage

"When his conscience accused him, the Witness of the Spirit, joined to the promises of the word, assured him he was a child of God."

"The Witness of the Spirit is no inward voice with fresh information, but the Spirit's amen set upon Scripture in the believer's heart."

"Assurance rests on a threefold cord—the promises, the fruits of grace, and the Witness of the Spirit confirming both."
